title: Compact sample-driven SDK onramp and tool-call safety (WIP)
summary: Working draft: small, pragmatic PRD sketch for an SDK onramp that uses sample-driven shaping to reduce friction, plus a compact safety model for tool calls and progressive structured output when streaming. Focus is: make first-run SDK integration fast for app devs, keep streaming overhead tiny, and provide a deterministic safety/commit model for tool invocation paths.
goals: Enable a 10-minute dev loop for a basic streaming+tool-call integration (auto-generated client wiring from a few sample calls)
Provide a compact frame protocol and typed-lite schema that allows partial validation without large parsing costs on the client
Define a predictable safety/hedging model for tool calls so apps can reason about idempotency, retries, and side-effect rollback
Keep per-request overhead low: <2KB of handshake metadata for typical sessions and able to recover/resume after interruptions
user_stories: As a frontend engineer, I want the SDK to infer output schema from a few sample responses so I can render fields without writing a custom parser
As an infra engineer, I want deterministic retry/hedge semantics for tool calls so server-side effects are not duplicated during network flakiness
As a mobile dev, I want the streaming handshake to be tiny and resumeable so offline/poor-network UX stays great
As an SRE, I want telemetry hooks per-frame so we can attribute latency and cost to specific output phases
design_notes: High level decisions: 1) sample-driven onramp: client submits up to 3 example prompt/response pairs (or picks a canned sample) -> server returns a lightweight typed-stencil + validation hints. 2) Compact frame protocol: frames = {meta(utf8), delta(text/html/typed-json), commit} where meta is minimal. 3) Tool calls are represented as 'tool-ops' frames with explicit id and idempotency token. 4) SDK exposes optimistic, confirmed, and compensated call results. 5) Streaming partial-JSON: we stream typed fragments (field-level) instead of full JSON trees, enabling early render. Note: keep wire-format backward-compatible by versioning the frame type in the handshake.
streaming_behavior:
- Handshake: client sends sample bundle + client capabilities (streaming, delta-json, low-bandwidth)
- Server replies with session token + typed-stencil + small perf hints (suggested batch size, compact-encode)
- Streaming frames use sequence numbers and optional fragment-paths for partial JSON assembly
- Resume: client can request resume from last acked seq or request a snapshot id (compact, infrequent)
- Backpressure: client publishes consumption window; server respects latency budget by reducing batch sizes or falling back to text-mode
- Cost-control: server can emit 'fidelity_suggestion' frames (e.g., recommend shorter completions or turn on KV-prefetch).
tool_call_semantics:
- Tool-op frame: {tool_id, op_id, idempotency_token (opt), intent_metadata, estimated_cost_hint}
- States: optimistic -> in_flight -> confirmed | failed | compensated
- Idempotency: if op_id or idempotency_token repeats, server de-duplicates; SDK surface returns prior confirmed result if available
- Compensation hooks: for non-idempotent tools (external side-effects) server returns compensation suggestions (e.g., 'undo' op template) and a compensation-score. App teams responsible for enacting compensation; Redwood surface exposes guidance and a 'compensate' helper call for supported adapters.
- Hedging: for high-latency tool endpoints, SDK will allow 'parallel speculative-sibling' calls bounded by policy; default: disabled for private deployments, opt-in for hosted with quota checks.
- Safety: default reject list + schema-based sanitizer for arguments; enterprise customers can supply a validation webhook.
validation_and_fallback:
- Partial validation: typed-stencil contains field-level validators (type, regex, enum). Stencil is intentionally permissive: 'best-effort' checks only.
- Fallback path: if fragments cannot validate, stream a 'raw_text' frame and a 'post-process' suggestion.
- Schema evolution: stencil includes 'revision' and backward-compatibility hints; client can request strict or lenient mode.
- Tool call failure modes are explicit: 'no-op-retry' vs 'requires-manual' and surfaced via telemetry and SDK callbacks.
- Developer UX: include a dev-mode that shows raw frames, unvalidated fragments, and suggested mapping for quick iteration.
telemetry_and_sla:
- Per-frame metrics: seq, frame_type, server_latency_ms, parse_latency_ms, token_count 
- Tool-call metrics: op_id, end_to_end_ms, retries, compensation_invoked
- Goals: 95th percentile end-to-end stream fragment latency < 200ms for interactive tier on typical routes, tool-call median < 400ms (alpha target)
- Billing/Quota: compact frames counted differently; we annotate to the billing pipeline to keep costs transparent.
- Logging: provide opt-in verbose logs for beta customers. Ensure no PII leaked in default logs; use redact hooks.
rollout_plan:
1) Internal dogfood (eng + solutions) - gated feature flag, week-long playtests (Q4 2025)
2) Invite-only beta with 3 customers (focus: conversational agents with calendar / search tools) - 6 weeks, collect telemetry
3) Public beta with opt-in SDK 1.0 and migration guide - target Q1 2026
4) GA when latencies and safety metrics validated and feature parity for resume + idempotency achieved

Consideration: enterprise-private instances might need alternate handshake with longer TTLs and manual webhook validators.
open_questions: How aggressive should default hedging be for hosted customers vs private? (policy + cost tradeoffs)
What minimal set of sample pairs produces useful typed-stencils reliably across domains? (1..3?)
Should compensation helpers be first-class SDK calls or helper recipes (security implications)
Do we expose 'optimistic' tool outputs in the same event stream as guaranteed ones? timeline/ordering semantics need definition
How to represent complex nested outputs compactly (typed-fragment paths vs full delta-json) without confusing SDK consumers?
